briefing.opening: Good day. Welcome to the Climate Briefing for November 15, 2026. We bring you key developments regarding global climate disasters and the transition to carbon neutrality, focusing on the 31st UN Climate Change Conference of the Parties (COP31) currently taking place in Türkiye.

sections.title: 🔴 [Climate Disasters] Super El Niño and Extreme Drought Deepen the Global Survival Crisis
sections.content: At the COP31 summit currently underway in Antalya, Türkiye, a Super El Niño—assessed as the most powerful in at least 1,000 years—was highlighted as a grave threat magnifying disasters worldwide [105]. Severe drought has exposed dinosaur tracks in Texas, USA, and ancient Buddhist statues in China's Yangtze River, while Ahus Island in Papua New Guinea faces an existential crisis due to water depletion and food shortages [99, 103]. These extreme climate anomalies are disrupting global food security and dealing a direct blow to household grocery prices in South Korea, where the cost of imported Norwegian mackerel has surged sharply [20].

sections.title: 🌍 [International Summit Trends] COP31 Climate Negotiations Face Deepening Gridlock and Discord
sections.content: As the 31st UN Climate Change Conference of the Parties (COP31) opened with the Presidency urging decisive action, friction both inside and outside the negotiating halls surrounding climate science and implementation pathways has intensified [3, 98, 101, 104]. Concerns over a leadership vacuum in the international community are mounting alongside the rollback of U.S. climate programs, while host nation Türkiye itself grapples with severe water scarcity [92, 96, 100]. Furthermore, a tracker of 96 global climate action indicators released at the venue revealed that while renewable energy expansion has made some progress, efforts to cut methane—a potent greenhouse gas—and reduce food loss remain virtually stalled [80].

sections.title: ⚠️ [Domestic Policy Review] South Korea's Diplomatic Push Meets Backlash Over 'NDC Washing'
sections.content: At COP31, the South Korean government highlighted its achievements in ocean-based climate action, including blue carbon, accelerated preparations for the 2028 UN Ocean Conference in Busan, and signed a framework agreement on climate change cooperation with Nepal [1, 2, 7, 9, 102]. However, on the sidelines of the international talks, sharp criticism emerged that South Korea's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) amounts to mere 'NDC washing' due to its heavy reliance on overseas carbon offsets, while entirely sidelining youth voices [88]. South Korea also faced scrutiny for pouring 37 trillion KRW into overseas fossil fuel projects compared to just 7 trillion KRW for international climate finance, alongside contributing only 30% of its pledged funding to the Loss and Damage Fund, ranking 20th among donor nations [87].

sections.title: 🌱 [Industry & Civic Action] Decarbonization Tech Innovation and the Surge of Grassroots Action
sections.content: While the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI) delegation showcased Korean corporate innovations in carbon neutrality and urged supportive policy measures at COP31, Pulmuone presented a sustainable dietary model achieving a 30% reduction in carbon emissions solely through dietary adjustments [16, 18, 51]. Meanwhile, the government is moving forward with a 2.8 trillion KRW investment in renewable energy financing and deployment, and major domestic battery makers attended a North American renewable energy exhibition to establish technical partnerships targeting the power market for AI data centers [68, 70, 79]. At the local level, grassroots climate initiatives continue to gain momentum: students from Sangju Girls' High School evaluated local government carbon neutrality plans to propose policy reforms directly to the council, and 1,500 citizens mobilized in Daejeon to accelerate community solar adoption [37, 48, 67].

briefing.closing: The climate crisis directly targets our food, energy, and fundamental survival, and building international trust is impossible without tangible emissions cuts and financial support. It is time to move beyond empty rhetoric to accountable, on-the-ground climate action. This concludes today's Daily Climate Briefing.
